newsitem.title: UK: Business feels vulnerable to defections - survey.
newsitem.headline: Business feels vulnerable to defections - survey.

text.p: Top directors of "people businesses", including many in the financial sector such as investment banking, feel vulnerable to defections by key staff, a survey by City law firm Theodore Goddard showed on Monday.

"The People Business - A New Legal Frontier", a survey of 120 senior directors of top 1,000 companies, revealed that 70 percent feel their business is only as good as its people and that 90 percent are worried about theft of advice.

The question of staff defections and the possible legal ramifications was thrown into sharp relief last week with the controversy over star Deutsche Morgan Grenfell fund manager Nicola Horlick who resigned amid allegations that she had tried to defect to a rival bank with a team of colleagues.
But while many directors acknowledge the importance of people to their business the survey shows thay have little idea on how to calculate their worth.
"Astonishingly, over half of (the) sample thought it impossible to accurately asses the value of staff when acquiring or selling a business," the survey, carried out by NOP said.
Theodore Goddard partner Jayesh Patel, an expert on City law, cites the case of Barings, the British investment bank brought low in 1995 after massive unauthorised trading in the Far East.
Patel says the attraction for the buyer of Barings, Dutch financial group ING, was "the perceived ability of ING to tap new markets through the contacts of the existing Barings staff."
This led ING to pay bonuses totalling between 90 and 100 million stg as the staff's loyalty was considered essential to maintain the value of the business, Patel says.

Two thirds of the respondents in the survey said that existing teams of staff were seen as more valuable than individuals -- the whole being greater than the sum of the parts -- but 78 percent also agreed that, given the goodwill based on client relationships, great damage can be done by scorned staff.

"There are clear implications for banks which are financing a merger or acquisition -- if the staff in the business are a key part of its value but they are not effectively locked in, the bank is left in a vulnerable position," Patel said.
He concludes that loyalty in staff has been replaced, in the most part, by financial motivation.
"The City is a people industry," Patel says. "It is all to do with people, it is not even the business itself that matters. It is the contacts."
